claims.text: The controlled intervention is post-deposition annealing at 400–600 °C for 1–3 hours.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons have small grains.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons have high defect density.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons have significant lattice strain.
Annealing at 400–600 °C for 1–3 hours will increase grain size and reduce grain-boundary density.
The annealing treatment will reduce defect density.
The annealing treatment will reduce lattice strain.
Grain coarsening and reduced structural disorder will produce a more uniform magnetic-domain structure with less boundary pinning.
Reducing structural heterogeneity will minimize local variations in exchange interactions.
The annealed microstructure will facilitate easier and more coherent domain-wall motion.
Easier domain-wall motion will reduce magnetic hysteresis losses in the annealed samples.
Annealed samples will have a sharper magnetization transition and a more pronounced entropy-change peak than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will enhance the low-field magnetocaloric response.
Annealing will slightly increase refrigerant capacity at low applied fields.
Fine grains and defect-induced inhomogeneity in the as-deposited baseline produce larger hysteresis.
Lattice strain and defect-induced inhomogeneity in the as-deposited baseline broaden the magnetic phase transition and reduce magnetocaloric efficiency.
The maximum magnetic-cooling cycle frequency will remain limited by thin-film heat-transfer rates.
Annealing beyond 600 °C or for excessive durations may induce unwanted phase separation.
Competing phase transformations or excessive microstructural coarsening may alter the magnitude or direction of the annealing response.

Failure to obtain both the predicted magnetic improvement and corroborating microstructural change relative to an as-deposited control would falsify the proposed microstructural-homogenization mechanism.
